seed_results.text: This manuscript describes our approach for the Visual Dialog Challenge 2018. We use an ensemble of three discriminative models with different encoders and decoders for our final submission. Our best performing model on 'test-std' split achieves the NDCG score of 55.46 and the MRR value of 63.77, securing third position in the challenge.

block.text: This manuscript describes our approach for the Visual Dialog Challenge 2018. We use an ensemble of three discriminative models with different encoders and decoders for our final submission. Our best performing model on 'test-std' split achieves the NDCG score of 55.46 and the MRR value of 63.77, securing third position in the challenge.

block.text: Introduction

seed_results.text: Visual dialog BIBREF0 is an interesting new task combining the research efforts from Computer Vision, Natural Language Processing and Information Retrieval. While BIBREF1 presents some tips and tricks for VQA 2.0 Challenge, we follow their guidelines for the Visual Dialog challenge 2018. Our models use attention similar to BIBREF2 to get object level image representations from Faster R-CNN model BIBREF3. We experiment with different encoder mechanisms to get representations of conversational history.

seed_results.text: Common to all the models, we initialize our embedding matrix with pre-trained Glove word vectors of 300 dimensions using 6B tokens . Out of 11319 tokens present in the dataset, we found 188 tokens missing from the pre-trained Glove embeddings, so we manually map these tokens to words conveying semantically similar meaning, e.g. we map over ten variations of the word “yes” - misspelled or not picked up by tokenizer - “*yes", “yesa", “yess", “ytes", “yes-", “yes3", “yyes", “yees", etc.

seed_results.text: For image features, we extract Faster R-CNN features with ResNet-101 backbone trained on Visual genome BIBREF4 dataset, similar to BIBREF2. We use an adaptive number of object proposals per-image ranging from 10 to 100 generated using a fixed confidence threshold and each object is then associated with 2048-dimensional mean-pooled features using ROI pooling. We use discriminative decoding throughout our models.

seed_results.text: Conclusion

block.text: Conclusion

seed_results.text: We experimented with discriminative models for our submission. Object level image representations gave a huge uplift in the evaluation metrics. Bi-directional GRUs constantly performed better than uni-directional LSTMs with Memory Networks outperforming Late fusion encoders for encoding conversational history. We even found that fine-tuning Glove embeddings performed better than their counterparts. Our final submission is an ensemble of three discriminative models and achieve the NDCG of 55.46 on test-std.

Visual dialog BIBREF0 is an interesting new task combining the research efforts from Computer Vision, Natural Language Processing and Information Retrieval. While BIBREF1 presents some tips and tricks for VQA 2.0 Challenge, we follow their guidelines for the Visual Dialog challenge 2018. Our models use attention similar to BIBREF2 to get object level image representations from Faster R-CNN model BIBREF3. We experiment with different encoder mechanisms to get representations of conversational history.

Late fusion encoder BIBREF0 with concatenated history. We use two-layered LSTMs with 512 hidden units for embedding questions and history. The object-level features are weighed using only question embeddings. The word embeddings from Glove vectors are frozen and are not fine-tuned. Figure FIGREF6 gives an overview of the architecture.

Common to all the models, we initialize our embedding matrix with pre-trained Glove word vectors of 300 dimensions using 6B tokens . Out of 11319 tokens present in the dataset, we found 188 tokens missing from the pre-trained Glove embeddings, so we manually map these tokens to words conveying semantically similar meaning, e.g. we map over ten variations of the word “yes” - misspelled or not picked up by tokenizer - “*yes", “yesa", “yess", “ytes", “yes-", “yes3", “yyes", “yees", etc.

We experimented with discriminative models for our submission. Object level image representations gave a huge uplift in the evaluation metrics. Bi-directional GRUs constantly performed better than uni-directional LSTMs with Memory Networks outperforming Late fusion encoders for encoding conversational history. We even found that fine-tuning Glove embeddings performed better than their counterparts. Our final submission is an ensemble of three discriminative models and achieve the NDCG of 55.46 on test-std.

Visual dialog BIBREF0 is an interesting new task combining the research efforts from Computer Vision, Natural Language Processing and Information Retrieval. While BIBREF1 presents some tips and tricks for VQA 2.0 Challenge, we follow their guidelines for the Visual Dialog challenge 2018. Our models use attention similar to BIBREF2 to get object level image representations from Faster R-CNN model BIBREF3. We experiment with different encoder mechanisms to get representations of conversational history.

Late fusion encoder BIBREF0 with concatenated history. We use two-layered LSTMs with 512 hidden units for embedding questions and history. The object-level features are weighed using only question embeddings. The word embeddings from Glove vectors are frozen and are not fine-tuned. Figure FIGREF6 gives an overview of the architecture.

We experimented with discriminative models for our submission. Object level image representations gave a huge uplift in the evaluation metrics. Bi-directional GRUs constantly performed better than uni-directional LSTMs with Memory Networks outperforming Late fusion encoders for encoding conversational history. We even found that fine-tuning Glove embeddings performed better than their counterparts. Our final submission is an ensemble of three discriminative models and achieve the NDCG of 55.46 on test-std.

Common to all the models, we initialize our embedding matrix with pre-trained Glove word vectors of 300 dimensions using 6B tokens . Out of 11319 tokens present in the dataset, we found 188 tokens missing from the pre-trained Glove embeddings, so we manually map these tokens to words conveying semantically similar meaning, e.g. we map over ten variations of the word “yes” - misspelled or not picked up by tokenizer - “*yes", “yesa", “yess", “ytes", “yes-", “yes3", “yyes", “yees", etc.
